images.alt: An Acorn BBC Micro Model B keyboard computer photographed from the front, showing its function keys and red keyboard trim
images.caption: The BBC Micro Model B, as it shipped in December 1981: 32 KB of memory, a full complement of ports, and BBC BASIC in ROM.
images.author: simon.inns

images.alt: An Acorn BBC Model B computer displayed at a retrocomputing exhibition, shown at an angle
images.caption: Acorn expected to sell twelve thousand of these. It sold well over a million, most of them into British schools.
images.author: Soupmeister

images.alt: The rear panel of a BBC Micro Model B, showing its array of analogue, user, printer, and expansion ports
images.caption: Every port on the back was documented and meant to be wired to something: an analogue port, a user port, a printer port, and the Tube.
images.author: Barney Livingston

images.alt: A BBC Micro Model B fitted with a second-processor expansion board carrying an ARM7TDMI chip, connected via the Tube interface
images.caption: The Tube interface let a second processor take over as the main CPU. Acorn's own next processor, the ARM, was first developed on a board plugged in here.
images.author: Trevor Johnson from Bristol, UK
